en: Homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers,
wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas.

Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by *kinnaras*, *mahoragas*, and so forth; by gods, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, *asuras*, *garuḍas*, *kinnaras*, and *mahoragas*; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with the community of his disciples, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now at that time, there lived in Śrāvastī a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who was wealthy, of great fortune and vast possessions, with extensive and wide-ranging holdings; he was endowed with wealth equal to Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the riches of Vaiśravaṇa.
He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant. After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a daughter was born.

She was beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs; having been raised and nurtured, she grew up to be a mature woman, and her kinsmen gave her the name Sumāgadhā.

Now, in the city of Puṇḍravardhana, there lived a householder named Mūṣila, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property, and whose wealth equaled that of Vaiśravaṇa.
He had a son named Vṛṣabhadatta,
who was handsome, pleasing to behold, gracious, and endowed with all major and minor limbs; however,
due to association with followers of other sects, he became devoted to the Nirgranthas.

When the Blessed One displayed the miracle of supernatural power regarding the unsurpassed human dharma, all the other non-Buddhist teachers were broken and defeated; they retreated to the borderlands,
some to the village of Gauḍika and others to the city of Puṇḍravardhana.
Some [went] to the city of Bhadrika.
That householder’s son remained in a state of dejection, and he was addressed by the Nirgranthas:
"Why do you not marry us? He replied, "I have no wife who is my equal. They said, "Anāthapiṇḍada has a daughter named Sumāgadhā."
"She too was beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and like the most beautiful woman in the land; therefore, seek her out.
Upon hearing this, his mind became filled with passion for her immediately. Then, having assumed the garb of a follower of another sect, he eventually arrived at Śrāvastī.

While wandering for alms, he entered the house of Anāthapiṇḍada. Sumāgadhā came out having taken some alms-food; she was seen by him, and at the mere sight of her, his mind became intensely impassioned. With a confused mind, he took up some parched grain in his bowl.
And [the food] was churned in a winnowing basket.

Then, seeing him with his sense faculties unrestrained, Sumāgadhā laughed and said, "These followers of other sects accept almsfood without clear comprehension. Thereupon, he too, laughing along with her, took the almsfood and departed.

Then, having gone to Puṇḍravardhana, he informed his father. By him, that girl was requested after going to Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Householder, this is not to be done by one who has gone forth. However, if Sumāgadhā goes to Puṇḍravardhana..."
"Even there, he will perform the work of a Buddha.
Then, with great magnificence, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada gave Sumāgadhā to Vṛṣabhadatta,
who led her to his own home.
Then, at another time, while the Nirgranthas were eating in that house,
she was told by her mother-in-law: "Daughter,
come and see the ones worthy of offerings."
The thought occurred to her:
"Surely the great śrāvakas, headed by the elders Ārya Śāradvatīputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and Ārya Ānanda, have been invited. Delighted and joyful, she went out.

Having seen those Nirgranthas—stained like the feathers of a crow, their garments covered in layers of filth, their bodies foul-smelling, naked, and resembling hungry ghosts—she became despondent once again.
Her mother-in-law said to her, "Daughter,
why are you so distressed? She replied, "Noble lady,
if such as these are worthy of offerings, what then must those who commit evil deeds be like?"
She said: "Girl, is there any teacher in the world other than these who is more distinguished? She replied:
"In Śrāvastī, in my father’s monastery, there is that Blessed One who is pure on both his mother's and father's side,
a Kṣatriya by birth,
having gone forth from a royal family of the lineage of universal monarchs."

He has gone forth from a high family, not a low one. Furthermore, that Blessed One has gone forth from a wealthy family, not a destitute one. Furthermore, that Blessed One is young, youthful, and endowed with fresh vigor.
At the time when one ought to dwell devoted to play, joy, adornment, decoration, and worldly pursuits— at that very moment,

while his kinsmen were against their will, with throats choked with tears and faces weeping, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron-colored robes, and out of genuine faith went forth from the home to the homeless life. Furthermore:

The Blessed One was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; his body was radiant with the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), adorned with a fathom-wide aura of light, and possessed a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, he was auspicious in every way, handsome, beautiful to behold, and inspiring.
Having understood and seen this, the Blessed One teaches the Dharma to his disciples with its underlying cause, not without its cause;
with its means of escape, not without its means of escape.
It is with its progression, not without its progression;
it is with its recourse, not without its recourse;
it is with its prowess, not without its prowess.
It was accompanied by miracles, not devoid of miracles.
The Blessed One is possessed of wisdom, one of great insight; he is fully capable of refuting, in accordance with the Dharma, those opposing disputants who have arisen.
The Blessed One is one who establishes his own doctrine; he is a proponent of karma, a proponent of action.
The Blessed One is the first to speak and speaks with kindness.
With a bright facial complexion, free from frowns, and preceded by a smile; saying "Come" and "Welcome," the Blessed One is one whose speech is auspicious and who possesses external grace;
the Blessed One is a speaker of varied discourse and a speaker of sweet words.
Possessing auspicious vows, he was compassionate toward the welfare of many and had trained a vast multitude of people.
By means of the noble Dharma, the Dharma of justice, the stainless Dharma, and the incomparable Dharma, that Blessed One had found companions;
his many companions were perfected in ethical discipline, perfected in concentration, perfected in wisdom, perfected in liberation, and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore,
whatever village or field that Blessed One dwells in dependence upon,
neither humans nor non-humans cause him any harm there.
From time to time, divine forms are seen,
divine sounds are heard,
and sublime radiances are perceived.
"The god, from time to time, duly bestows a stream of rain.
Upon merely hearing this, her mind became serene toward the Blessed One;
with a serene mind, she said: "Daughter,"
"Can you show that Blessed One to us? She replied, "Noble lady, in that case, please prepare the meal."
"Tomorrow I shall bring the Blessed One," she said. Mūṣila’s wife replied, "Excellent;
everything is prepared.
Then Sumāgadhā ascended to the roof of the palace, smeared a circular mandala, scattered flowers, and having paid homage to the Blessed One, [she faced] in the direction where he was dwelling.
She scatters flowers in every direction,
offers incense,
and sends water from a pitcher as an invitation to the Blessed One. She speaks thus:
O Omniscient One, O Compassionate One, please grant me your vision now; come here yourself! O Conqueror of Enemies, dwell this incomparable night together with the Saṅgha, which is like the ocean.
O Blessed One, for the sake of favoring me today, and to bring peace to the minds of men,
let your grace be bestowed, O Sole Lord of the World, by the mere sight of your form.
Then, through the supernatural power of the Buddhas and the supernatural power of the deities, those flowers set out toward the Jeta Grove through the sky like a flight of swans;
and the incense, like a mass of clouds, stood before the Blessed One as a canopy of beryl rods.
Seeing this, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One:
"From where, Blessed One, has this invitation come?
"From Puṇḍravardhana, Ānanda."
"Sixty-one hundred yojanas [from here]. Go, Ānanda, and announce to the monks:
'Tomorrow you must go to the city of Puṇḍravardhana.'"
One should perform a display of supernatural power over that city occupied by the non-Buddhists,
for the purpose of inspiring faith in those who lack it and increasing the faith of those who already possess it.
"For the restraint of those who are difficult to manage, and for the comfortable dwelling of those who possess a sense of shame.

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having struck the ghaṇṭī and assembled the community of monks, he stood at the head of the elders and, while distributing the voting sticks (*śalākā*), spoke thus:
"Listen, venerable sirs;
the Blessed One commands the Saṅgha:
'Tomorrow you must go to the city of Puṇḍravardhana.'"
That city is occupied by heretics;
a display of supernatural power must be performed in order to inspire faith in those who lack it.
For the further increase of those who are already confident, for the restraint of the ill-behaved, and for the comfortable dwelling of those who possess a sense of shame.
Then the elder monks began to take up the voting sticks (*śalākā*). Among them was an elder named Pūrṇa, the son of Sukuṇḍa;
he too began to take up a voting stick. The Venerable Ānanda said to him: "Elder, you must not go to this house of Anāthapiṇḍada."
"However, we must go to the city of Puṇḍravardhana, a distance of one hundred and sixty *yojanas*, and perform a display of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*).
Thereupon, the Elder hurriedly cast his voting stick (*śalākā*),
until the voting stick was given to the second monk."
Having thus produced the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he extended his right arm, which was like the trunk of an elephant, took the tally-stick, and said:
"Neither by the qualities of physical form, nor by beauty, nor by the quality of force, nor out of respect;
rather, those whose youth has been crushed by old age become like me—possessors of the six supernormal powers."
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the elder monks set out, each by means of his own supernatural power.
Now, Mūṣila’s wife, having prepared pure and excellent food and drink for the sake of the Blessed One, having arranged seats and set out a water-jar, [waited].
Having ascended to the roof of the palace, Sumāgadhā also stood outside with her husband and father-in-law, and she thought:
"Will the Blessed One come? Or will he not come? Or perhaps he has been invited elsewhere?"

Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One, she began to look toward the direction in which he resided. In the meantime, the venerable Ājñāta-kaundinya, having manifested a chariot of serpents, sat upon it slowly and very gently while it rained down, lightning flashed forth, and the roar of thunder resounded above.
He came through the air by means of supernatural power.
Seeing him, the master of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this your Teacher?"

"This person, seated upon a snake-chariot, approaching through the sky by means of supernatural power with the deep roar of thunderclouds, displaying flashes of lightning as it rains gently and slowly—
this is not the noble Ajñātakauṇḍinya, the elder of the Saṅgha. She said this.

"When the Dharma was being taught by the Blessed One at Vārāṇasī, he first attained freedom from passion; this Blessed One designated him as the foremost among those who have attained the realization of Nirvāṇa, and here he is coming.
(1) In the meantime, the Venerable Śāriputra, having manifested a lion-chariot and seated upon it, came through the sky above by means of his supernatural power.
Seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that teacher of yours who is coming in the lion-chariot?
She replied:
"This is not the noble Śāriputra, who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of wisdom.
While he was still in the womb, all the debaters in Jambudvīpa were defeated by his mother."
And by him a longing was produced in his mother:
"Would that I might climb to the summit of Mount Sumeru and drink the water of all four oceans.

Then Tiṣya, the most excellent of the twice-born, having summoned Hari—an expert in the art of sorcery who had reached the further shore of *indrajāla*—in an assembly of men, gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, gandharvas, and yakṣas...
The queen’s pregnancy longing was thus satisfied.
And when he had emerged from his mother’s womb, his father summoned all the experts in omens and said to them: "May you examine him."
"What will be the power of the prince? they asked.

They began to examine him; and having seen the excellence of the prince's marks and the excellence of his form, they were struck with supreme wonder, yet they were unable to declare, "This is the power of the prince."
Then, from the sky, in order to dispel their doubt, a great brahmin proclaimed with a brahmin’s voice:

"This youth, having gone forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Śākyamuni, will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions and will become the foremost among all disciples."
He is the one who turns the wheel of Dharma.

Now, even the debaters, having gazed upon his face, do not utter even a word they have long desired; how much less, then, would they engage in debate? Regarding the performance of debate, the Blessed One spoke thus:
The volume of ink would be equal to the great ocean; the weight of birch-bark leaves would be equal to Mount Sumeru;
and the number of scribes would be equal to the total number of sentient beings in the four continents.

The measure of the grass, wood, branches, leaves, and seeds of this earth might reach total exhaustion through successive succession, but I do not say there is any exhaustion of this Śāriputra’s wisdom. Therefore, he is designated as "of great wisdom," like a great caravan leader. His wisdom is the most excellent among all sentient beings, reaching even unto all humans, gods, and asuras dwelling in the three worlds.
The wisdom of all the world, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s,
does not equal even a sixteenth part of Śāriputra’s wisdom.
Furthermore, it was said:

on the occasion of the discourse concerning the method for distinguishing the concise and detailed aspects of the Four Noble Truths, [it was stated]: "In this world, there is no one equal to him among those who have arisen, not even a Pratyekabuddha;
he is now approaching. (2)
In the meantime, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having miraculously manifested a golden mountain— filled with various herds of wild animals,
abounding in various springs, crowded with various flocks of birds, and adorned with various trees— sat upon it and approached through the air above by means of his supernatural power.
Seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that teacher of yours who comes having ascended the Golden Mountain?
She replied:
"This is not the noble Mahākāśyapa, who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those of few desires, those who are contented, and those who maintain the ascetic virtues (dhūtaguṇa).
By him, nine hundred and ninety-nine ploughs [were pulled] by a hundred thousand oxen."
Sixty crores of gold pieces made of refined gold, eighty khāris of barley,
and sixteen villages of slaves.
Having renounced eighteen villages of great devotees, as well as many hundreds of thousands of articles and requisites, he went forth into homelessness.
Furthermore:
In the presence of all the śrāvakas, this one was invited by the Blessed One to share half his seat.
"A single measure of rice is better;
a single bed brings happiness."
A pair of fine garments is to be avoided; singing is the embrace of delusion.

Thinking thus, he accepted everything except that which was called "non-possession," which he did not take. And he who, having abandoned his sister’s daughter—who was beautiful, lovely to behold, and like the most beautiful woman in the land—went forth into homelessness, he is now approaching. (3) At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw him, walking with the graceful gait of the noble elephant Airāvaṇa, endowed with the marks and signs of supreme natural character, and pleasing to behold due to his merit.
Having manifested himself as an elephant and seated upon it, he came through the sky by means of his supernatural power.
Seeing him, the lord of Sumāgadhā asked: "Sumāgadhā, is this that Teacher of yours who is coming in a chariot drawn by the king of elephants?"
She said:
"This is not the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of those possessed of supernatural powers."
By this [merit], Śakra, the lord of the gods, [obtained] the Vaijayanta palace,
measuring one thousand yojanas in circumference and firmly established upon eighty-four thousand pillars.
These five and a half *yojanas* [from the city of the gods] were shaken by the big toe as he rose up;
and the two Naga kings named Nanda and Upananda, having encircled Sumeru with their coils, remained there in a state of disciplined submission.
Furthermore, the Blessed One was addressed by him in this way:
For thus, venerable sir, in Vaijayanta there is famine, hardship, and a wilderness; alms-food is difficult for a beggar to obtain,
and even the monks are exhausted by meager food.
"Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One and have received it directly from him: 'In this great earth, there exists an exquisite element of flavor situated beneath.'"
SumAv_71: "Therefore, I wish for the king to bring forth the exquisite essence-element from this great earth, so that what is above may be brought below, and what is below may be brought above.
SumAv_72: The Blessed One said:
"Standing in what place do you overturn the great earth?
He replied:
"I shall overturn the great earth from the position between the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains."
The Blessed One said:
"What will you do with those living beings who depend upon the earth? He replied:
"I shall lift up those living beings who depend upon the earth with my left hand and hold them."
"With my right hand, I shall overturn the great earth. The Blessed One said:
"What will your perception be? [He replied: "It will be just like this:"
"Venerable sir,
just as a strong man, while turning over a plantain leaf, perceives it as extremely light,
even so do I, venerable sir."
"Thinking, 'I shall turn the great earth over and perceive it as extremely light,' [he said],
'Excellent, excellent, Maudgalyāyana!'"
"Are you able, by means of this supernatural power and through this method, to overturn the great earth? She was then approaching.

(4) In the meantime, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having miraculously created a crystal gabled chamber—covered with emeralds, adorned with pillars of various jewels, and beautified by coral railings—arranged therein a couch spread with cotton cloth, woolen rugs, embroidered coverlets, and stuffed mattresses.
As far as the red cushions, he sat there and then came through the air above by means of his supernatural power.
Seeing him, the master of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā,..."
"That teacher of yours is this one who, having manifested a gabled chamber made of crystal, sits therein and comes through the sky above by means of supernatural power.
She said,
"This is not the noble Mahākātyāyana."
"The Blessed One has declared this man to be the foremost among those who analyze the sūtras and possess great power through merit;
here he comes.
(5) At that moment, the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, having manifested a chariot drawn by bulls, sat upon it and approached through the sky above by means of his supernatural power.
Seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that Teacher of yours who is coming by means of a bull-chariot?
She replied:
"This is not the noble Mahākauṣṭhila, who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of those with few desires. SumAv 83:
He spoke thus to the monks:
Venerable friends, more than eighty years have passed since I went forth into homelessness.
"I do not recall ever having accepted service from my fellow celibates, even so much as the rubbing of their backs;
yet here he comes.
(6) In the meantime, the Venerable Upāli miraculously created a golden palm grove, endowed with golden flowers and fruits, and filled with various delightful sounds.
There, his body unimpeded, he came through the air by means of supernatural power.

Seeing him, the master of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that Teacher of yours who, having taken recourse to the golden palm grove, comes through the air by means of supernatural power?"
She said:
"Noble one, this is not Upāli;
he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya."
SumAv_87: And before him, about five hundred Śākya youths, adorned with various ornaments and about to go forth into the religious life, made a great heap of garments and jewelry.
SumAv_88: This noble one reflected:
"These youths, endowed with noble lineage, wealth, and youth, have begun to go forth into the religious life, having cast aside their vast harems and their abundant treasuries and granaries."
"I was attached to mere ornaments;
thinking, 'By this I shall fall into calamity,' I abandoned that splendor like a globule of spittle, went forth into homelessness, and attained the state of an Arhat before anyone else.
He is coming here. (7)
In the meantime, the venerable Aśvajit, with a tranquil deportment, was taming a rutting elephant;
with bowl and robe held in his hands, he approached through the air above by means of his supernatural power.
Upon seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, [who is this?]"
"That teacher of yours is he who comes through the sky above by means of supernatural power, with his deportment so peaceful, his hands holding a bowl and a staff.
She replied,
"This is not the noble Aśvajit."
With a tranquil deportment, he tames the intoxicated elephant. From him, by means of this verse:
"The leader has proclaimed how the world's arising is caused by karma and afflictions, and likewise the cause for the cessation of karma and afflictions."
In that state where the suffering inevitably caused by birth, old age, and decline does not abide—
that supreme liberation— the Primordial Bull, having realized it himself, proclaims it.
Having previously heard that the noble Śāriputra had attained the fruit of stream-entry and was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of mindfulness,
he is now approaching.
(8) In the meantime, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, having miraculously created a golden lotus with a thousand petals, [proceeded].
Seated upon a golden lotus the size of a cartwheel, with a stalk of beryl and filaments of diamond sprouts, he was traveling through the sky above by means of his supernatural power.

Seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that teacher of yours who, having manifested a golden thousand-petaled lotus the size of a cartwheel with a stalk of beryl and filaments of diamond sprouts, is seated there traveling through the sky above?"
She said:
"Noble Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra has not come;
he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who practice loving-kindness."
He is coming here.

(9) In the meantime, the venerable Dravya Mallaputra, having miraculously manifested a mountain peak composed of the four jewels, filled with the sound of various bells and adorned with various banners and flags, sat upon it and approached through the sky by means of his supernatural power.

Seeing him, the master of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that Teacher of yours, who, having miraculously created a mountain peak composed of the four jewels, covered with the ringing of various bells and adorned with various flags and banners, sits there above in the sky?"
She said:
"This noble Dravya Mallaputra is not he who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who dwell in secluded places."
"He who thus enjoins the monks who are resting to engage in meditative seclusion—

he is coming here. (10) In the meantime, the Venerable Aniruddha, having miraculously created a palace made entirely of gold, adorned with pillars of beryl and coral, variegated with various jewels, and decorated with canopies and garlands—
Adorned with a hundred banners in its center,
he sat within it and traveled through the sky above by means of supernatural power.
Seeing him, the lord of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that teacher of yours, who, having manifested a golden palace,
sits upon a lion-throne within it and comes through the sky by means of supernatural power?"
She said:
"This is not the noble Aniruddha;
he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of those with the divine eye."

SumAv_102: By this offering of a single alms-meal to a Pratyekabuddha while he was seated in Vārāṇasī, he exercised sovereignty as a Cakravartin king seven times, and seven times he exercised sovereignty over the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
SumAv_103: By the remainder of that very same karma, he was born into a wealthy Śākya family.
Having renounced many hundreds of thousands, even millions, of gold, silver, and bullion, he went forth into homelessness;
and having gone forth, he has become a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Furthermore, hear of his greatness:
Māhānāman was addressed by his mother: "Son,
the king has had a proclamation made by the sounding of a bell,
that the Śākyas must go forth into the religious life one family at a time."
"Therefore, you should go forth into the religious life.
He replied, "I will not go forth. My beloved son, who sits upon a comfortable seat on the upper floor of the palace, [is my joy]."
"Let him go forth into the religious life.
His mother said: "Son, he is one of great merit and power."
"Do not compete with him.
Mother, you have placed your faith in him because he is renowned for his great merit. Today, do not send him anything; I shall find out whether he is truly renowned for his great merit or not.
"Son, do so and verify it for yourself."
She filled a basket with those empty jars, covered it with a white cloth, marked it with a seal, and sent it in the hand of a maidservant, instructing her: "Daughter,
if anyone should ask you what is inside here,"
"Nothing need be said," she replied. Taking him, she set out.
Now, Śakra, the lord of the gods, exercises his vision and knowledge from below; he perceived:
"Indeed, by this woman, a Pratyekabuddha was provided with almsfood above."
"How could there be an obstacle to his meal today? His meal must be provided. With this thought, he filled that basket with food consisting of various soups, side dishes, and main courses.
Then, when the girl took it and went to Aniruddha, he said to her: "Girl,"
"What is there here? She replied, "Prince, there is nothing. Aniruddha reflected:
"I am dear to my mother; why would she [say such a thing]?"
"He will send it empty. Surely we must see what kind of food has been placed here.
When the [box] was opened, that entire garden was found to be filled with various implements and fragrant scents. Upon smelling them, Aniruddha was struck with great wonder:
"This man is devoted to his mother!"
By this means, he sent his mother the finest portion of food. He also instructed her, saying, "Mother, you ought to send such food every day.
Upon seeing this, she was filled with the utmost amazement. She pointed it out to Mahānāma, saying, "Son,"
"Have you seen it, Mother?
I have seen it. Did I not tell you previously: 'A being of great merit and renown, a fortunate human being'?"
"Do not engage in rivalry with him. He is now approaching. And he said:
"In a golden celestial palace, beautifully arranged and adorned with the radiance of jewels..."
Meditating, devoted to meditation, seated upon the auspicious dust-free throne, self-restrained—here comes the noble sage Aniruddha, whose banner is ever-steadfast;
he is liberated himself and is the liberator of the world submerged helplessly in the ocean of existence. (11)

In the meantime, the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, having miraculously created a pavilion of flowers, sat there and approached through the sky by means of his supernatural power while traveling above in the air.

Seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this that teacher of yours who, having miraculously created a pavilion of flowers, sits there and approaches through the sky by means of his supernatural power while traveling above in the air?"
She said:
"This is not the noble Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa; he is the one whom the Blessed One has designated as the foremost among those of little passion."
He was born with an earring set with jewels fastened upon his ear. His parents were struck with great wonder.

if you do not come,
I myself shall come accompanied by a great flood of troops."
All of that was communicated and reported to Mahākapphiṇa by means of a messenger.
SumAv_193: This King Kapphiṇ, surrounded by eighteen thousand ministers, entered Śrāvastī and proceeded into the Jetavana;
upon seeing him, whatever pride he had regarding his physical form and whatever pride he had regarding his sovereignty vanished.
"Even now, the pride of Bala is still being slain.
Then the Blessed One produced a worldly thought: "O, would that Śakra, the lord of the gods, were to come here taking up the bow of Indra!"

Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, Śakra, the lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One in the guise of a charioteer and presented him with Indra’s bow. When the Blessed One took up that bow which had been presented,
he was not even able to lift it, much less string it.
Then the Blessed One manifested seven iron drums; having himself strung that bow in the shape of a crescent moon, he discharged an arrow by which the seven iron drums were pierced,
and from them a sound emerged.
Exert yourselves!
Go forth!
Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.
"For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering."
That sound reached as far as the Akaniṣṭha gods, and consequently, his pride in his strength vanished.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his mind, caused his royal attire to disappear and taught him the Dharma; by means of which, he and his retinue of eighteen thousand ministers attained the fruit of stream-entry.
He realized it directly; having seen the truth, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One. Here he comes.

(17) In the meantime, the Venerable Ānanda, having miraculously created a park resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds, sat there in the sky above.

Seeing him, the husband of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, is this your Teacher, who, having miraculously created a grove resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds, sits there and comes through the sky above by means of his supernatural power? She replied: SumAv_203: She said:
This is not the noble Ānanda,
who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who guard the doors of their sense faculties.
Furthermore, he is four finger-breadths shorter than the Blessed One, yet he is golden-hued and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

By this act, he offered the middle parasol upon the stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa. As the ripening of that karma, he has enjoyed two thousand five hundred reigns as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);
had he not gone forth into homelessness now, he would have exercised the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch even at this time.
Yet, he has been made to go forth by the Blessed One through his power. Furthermore, he is the son of the Blessed One’s maternal aunt and is his brother. He is now approaching. (18)

In the meantime, the Venerable Rāhula manifested himself in the guise of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), endowed with the seven treasures, followed by eighty-four million divisions of the army, eighty-four thousand elephant-kings headed by the Nāga-king Upoṣadha,
eighty-four thousand horses headed by the horse-king Bālāhaka, and eighty-four thousand chariots headed by the chariot Nandīghoṣa.

Having caused it to be adorned with thousands of citizens and country folk, and with the sounds of various drums, conchs, and kettledrums, and beautified by raised banners and flags, he sat there and approached through the sky by means of his supernatural power.
Seeing him, the lord of Sumāgadhā asked Sumāgadhā: "Sumāgadhā, [who is this?]"
"That is your teacher,
he who comes in the guise of a wheel-turning monarch.
She said:
"This is not the noble Rāhula,
who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of those desiring training.
This is the son of the Blessed One, illuminating the glory abandoned by his father."
Displaying a supernatural power far more distinguished than that of any universal monarch (*cakravartin*), he came through the sky above by means of his miraculous power. And he said:
"Her splendor is garlanded with auspicious marks, most beautiful, rivaling the supernatural power of Śakra."
Having fashioned a vast palace endowed with the strength of a host of nāgas and adorned with the seven kinds of jewels,
the Son of the Buddha approaches through the sky; and this one,
known by the name Rāhula, is honored by the gods as he enters the residence of kings.
Some sages, having split the earth, move through it like water; others, emitting fire, swiftly appear like beautiful clouds pouring forth water clearly upon the world;
they assume the forms of Śakra, Brahmā, and Kubera, and possess the splendor of the moon, the sun, and the Daityas.
For those gentle ones, desiring the welfare of the world, have set forth through the sky.

He is now approaching. (19) While the community of monks had set out, at that moment the Tathāgata entered [the city]. The Blessed One attained such a state of meditative concentration that, as his mind was thus composed, rays of light issued forth from the Blessed One’s body.
That is to say, [the light] was blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, and crystal-colored;
by these, this world was illuminated with a sublime radiance, as far as Śrāvastī and as far as the city of Puṇḍravardhana.
In the interval between them, all people saw the Blessed One departing.
And there was a great earthquake.
Then Brahmā Sahāmpati, having known the Blessed One’s thought with his own mind, arrived together with the gods of the realm of form and stood at the Blessed One’s right side.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, also arrived together with the gods of the realm of desire and stood at his left side.
About five hundred gandharvas, headed by Tumburu and Supriya, arrived and performed services before the Blessed One with various kinds of instrumental music, song, and dance.
Many hundreds of thousands of deities followed closely behind him.
And from above, the apsarases showered the Blessed One with divine flowers—blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and māndārava blossoms.
They played divine musical instruments and scattered divine powders of agallochum, tagara, sandalwood, and tamāla leaves, and they waved their garments.
Now at that time, seven thousand sages were dwelling in a certain forest retreat.
Those sages beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, and graced by a fathom-wide halo of light.
With a radiance surpassing that of the sun,
like a moving mountain of jewels,
auspicious on all sides.
Like a sacrificial fire sprinkled with oblations,
like a lamp placed within a golden vessel,
he blazed with splendor like a sacrificial post of gold.
The proficiency of a mind practiced in *śamatha* for twelve years does not produce such [joy] as the first consecration of a king who delights in sovereignty,
or the obtaining of a son by one who is childless.
It is like a poor man finding a treasure, or like the first vision of a Buddha resulting from roots of merit that have been planted accordingly.
Then those sages approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and dispositions of those seers, delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, those seers shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Then those sages, having attended upon the Blessed Buddha, set out on their way.
At that time, there were eighteen gates in the city of Puṇḍravardhana.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"If I enter by the western gate,
there will be a change in the feelings of the city-dwellers residing at the other gates;
what if I were to manifest eighteen Buddhas and enter myself through the western gate?"
Then the Blessed One, having manifested eighteen Buddhas, entered himself through the western gate.
Upon the Blessed One’s entry into the city, such wonders and marvels occurred, as did others:
namely, the elevated regions of the earth sank down, and the depressed regions rose up.
The stones, pebbles, and gravel are removed; low doorways become high,
and narrow spaces become wide.
The elephants trumpet, the horses neigh,
and the camels bray.
The cows lowed, the bulls bellowed with joy, and the peacocks uttered their cries.
Various musical instruments within the houses sounded of their own accord;
the blind regained their sight,
and the deaf heard.
The mute become capable of speech; those with impaired or deficient sense faculties regain their senses in full;
and those intoxicated by liquor or madness become sober.
Those who have drunk poison become free from poison;
those who are mutual enemies attain loving-kindness;
and pregnant women give birth safely.
Those bound in fetters were set free,
and the destitute obtained wealth.
With such splendor he entered and approached the residence of Sumāgadhā.
Then Sumāgadhā herself filled a water-jar with *gośīrṣa* sandalwood water and offered it for the washing of the feet of the Blessed One and the community of monks.
Thereupon, Sumāgadhā prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and said:
"Blessed are those who behold you, the crusher of the arguments of opposing disputants; they are blessed who behold your face."
Those who joyfully listen to the words of one seated in a vast assembly,
or he who shall salute you— the treasury of glory— with his head and both hands pressed together in humility, will attain great gain.
Then the Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Perceiving that the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, was comfortably seated, he personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent solid and soft foods.

Then the multitude of people living in Puṇḍravardhana, not seeing the Blessed One, began to break down that house. Thereupon, the Blessed One miraculously transformed that house into one made of crystal.
For the entire great multitude saw the Blessed One and the community of monks as if they were reflected in a mirror while eating.
And he said:
"That very delightful [hall] became made of crystal, variegated with the ornamentation of jewels, gold, and precious gems."
The entire population of the city gazes upon the moon-like Lord of Sages as if he were standing right before them.

With all their limbs bristling with horripilation from faith, men bowed to the moon-like Lord of Sages with palms joined and placed upon their heads, just as gods bow to Indra while he dwells within his celestial palace.
Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal, sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then the body of attendants headed by Sumāgadhā, those city-dwellers, those sages, and those gods, asuras, garuḍas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas [approached] the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One gave them such a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard it, some realized the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning,
and some the fruit of non-returning.
Some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions;
some produced the roots of goodness known as "heat"; and some produced the "summits."
Some developed the mild, medium, and intense levels of receptivity; some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; and some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Some resolved upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment; some took up the refuges; and some took up the precepts.
For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.
When this sutra had been spoken by the Blessed One, the monks said this to the Blessed One:
It is marvelous, Blessed One;
it is marvelous, Sugata, that Sumāgadhā, by relying on the Blessed One as her virtuous friend, has accomplished the work of a Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; listen to how in the past as well, having relied upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, as a spiritual friend, Kāñcanamālā performed the work of a Buddha."
"Pay close and careful attention; I shall speak.
Once upon a time, monks," SumAv_243: "In the past, monks."

In the past, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, and Blessed One.
He dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Now at that time, there was a king named Kṛkī.
A daughter was born to him with a golden garland bound upon her head;
therefore, her parents gave her the name Kāñcanamālā.
She was raised and nurtured until she became a grown woman; she became beloved, charming, dear, and pleasing to King Kṛkin.
Accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, she approached the Blessed One for an audience.
The Blessed One taught her the Dharma.
Having heard that Dharma, a great clarity of mind arose in her toward the Blessed One,
and she provided the Blessed One for as long as she lived with the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Now at that time, King Kṛkin saw ten dreams: (1) an elephant went out through a window, its tail remaining caught.
(2) A well runs dry behind a thirsty man as he flees.
(3) A prastha of pearls being sold for a prastha of barley meal. (4) Sandalwood being equated in price with common wood.
(5) A scent-elephant being terrified by young elephants;
(6) a grove abounding in flowers and fruits being plundered by those who take what is not given;
(7) a monkey smeared with filth smearing others.
(8) The consecration of the monkey king.
(9) A cloth is pulled by eighteen people, yet it does not tear.
(10) A great multitude of people gathers in one place, yet they do not spend their time in quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute.
Seeing him, he became afraid and terrified, thinking:
"Lest I be deprived of my kingdom or face a threat to my life on account of this.
Thereupon, the king summoned brahmins who were experts in the interpretation of dreams and informed them of his dream.
Seeing Kāñcanamālā, they said:
"O King, the sacrifice must be performed with the blood of her who is beloved by all the people;
the city must be encircled with her entrails."
"In this way, it will be for the welfare of Your Majesty;
having seen these terrible dreams that threaten both kingdom and life, by this means Your Majesty’s well-being shall be secured.
King [Bimbisāra] reflected:
Kāñcanamālā is dear to all people;
wishing to have her killed, the brahmins said this: "Death for me alone would be better, but I will not have Kāñcanamālā killed."
With his cheek resting on his hand, he remained lost in thought; Kāñcanamālā saw him and said,
"Why are you so lost in thought?"
"Your Majesty," he said.
He then related the matter in detail. She replied:
"This Blessed One, Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, is dwelling near Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana."
"Go to that Blessed One and ask him; whatever the Blessed One explains to you, hold it to be exactly so.
Then the king, accompanied by a great display of splendor and together with Kāñcanamālā, departed from Vārāṇasī and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Kāñcanamālā and hundreds of thousands of other brahmins and householders were also present.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Kṛkin with a discourse on the Dharma.
He inspired and gladdened them. Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, he became silent.
Then King Kṛkī, having reported the ten dreams, spoke thus: "Do not [be concerned] for me..."
“Venerable Sir, on that account there will be a fall from the kingdom and an obstacle to life.
The Blessed One said:
"Do not fear,
Great King;
on this account there shall be no loss of your kingdom nor any obstacle to your life."
(1) As for the dream you saw, O Great King,
of an elephant exiting through a window with its tail caught;
In a future time, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni.

Having completed all the work of a Buddha, he will pass into final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted. In the period after his final nirvāṇa, there will be Brahmins and householders who lack faith;
weeping and abandoning their tearful-faced kinsmen, they will go forth into homelessness and yet conceive the notion of "home" within the monasteries.
This is its precursor:
that you further saw in a dream a well running after a thirsty man from behind.
His very disciples will teach the Dharma to faithful householders,
yet they will depart still possessed of craving;
this is a foretoken of that.
(3) As for the dream you saw, in which a measure of barley-meal was being purchased with a measure of pearls:
it means that his disciples will, for the sake of that very measure of barley-meal, fully reveal the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
This is its precursor:
that you saw in a dream sandalwood being equated in price with common wood.
His very disciples, having accepted those words of the heretics, will harmonize them with the true Dharma; this is the omen of that which you saw in your dream. (5) As for the dream you beheld:
"The scent-elephant is being terrified by the young elephants"—
this is a precursor sign that his own disciples, being unrestrained, will expel those monks who possess virtuous conduct.

(6) As for the dream you saw, in which a monastery endowed with flowers and fruits was being plundered by those who take what is not given: that very monastery, having been dedicated to the noble Saṅgha of the disciples, was seized from the Saṅgha by certain individuals— uncultivated in body, uncultivated in mind, and uncultivated in wisdom— who made it their own resort and took away its flowers and fruits.
They will give [gifts] to their own kinsmen; this is its preliminary sign, that you have seen such a dream. (7) As for the dream which you saw:
"Just as a monkey smeared with filth smears others,

so too will his disciples— those who have not cultivated their bodies, have not cultivated their minds, and have not cultivated their wisdom— having fallen into transgression themselves, establish transgressions even for faithful monks;
this is a precursor to that."
(8) As for the dream you saw—
the consecration of a monkey to the kingship—
at that time even those with impaired faculties will become kings.
This is its precursor:
that you saw in your dream a cloth being pulled by eighteen people and yet not being torn.
After he has entered parinirvāṇa, his teaching will be divided into eighteen sects,
yet it will not be possible to tear the cloth of liberation;
this is its precursor.
(10) As for the dream you saw,
in which a great multitude of people gathered together and spent their time in quarreling, brawling, disputing, and contending—
that signifies that under his teaching, unrestrained monks will cause the disappearance [of the doctrine] through quarreling, brawling, contending, and disputing.
This is its precursor:
do not fear, O Great King.
"On this account, there shall be no loss of your kingdom nor any obstacle to your life.
Then the Blessed One gave such a Dharma teaching to that king and that great multitude of people, which penetrates the four noble truths,
that upon hearing it, eighty-four thousand living beings attained the vision of the truths.
SumAv_260: By means of Kāñcanamālā, having approached the Blessed One as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the work of a Buddha was accomplished.
SumAv_261: What do you think, monks? Is this Kāñcanamālā anyone else? She is none other than this Sumāgadhā.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Kāñcanamālā, such that she was reborn into a wealthy family and was born with a golden garland bound upon her head?"
The Blessed One said:
"It was by Kāñcanamālā alone,
monks."

Actions performed and accumulated in previous births—whose conditions have been met, whose causal factors have ripened, which have arrived like a rushing torrent, and which are inevitable—these were indeed performed and accumulated by Kāñcanamālā herself, O monks. Who else shall experience the results? No one else.
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Neither in the fire element nor in the wind element,
but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do the performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Long ago,
monks,
in the past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain poor woman.
Having tied a garland of various colorful straw and offered it at the stupa of a Pratyekabuddha, she made a prayer with a devout mind:
"By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of a gift, may I be born in whatever place I am reborn with a golden garland bound upon my head.
What do you think?
Monks, that poor woman was this very Kāñcanamālā. Because she made a vow with a devout mind,
for five hundred births she was born with a golden garland bound upon her head.
She untied two *paṇas* that were tied to the edge of her garment and gave them to the Noble Saṅgha;

thus, by the power of her vow, she was born into wealthy families. Then the Blessed One, having inspired faith in the great multitude of people residing in Puṇḍravardhana, headed by Sumāgadhā, departed.
In that very manner, together with his supernatural powers and the community of monks, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black."
For those that are exclusively white, it is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, it is mixed. Therefore, monks, [you should cultivate the mind that is exclusively white].
"Having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed,
one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white. Therefore,
monks,"
"Monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
"You should train yourselves thus.
The Blessed One spoke these words, and those monks, with joyful minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. Thus ends the *Sumāgadhāvadāna*.
